first.rationale: The two observed declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the same funnel stage, and memory_86 plus memory_31 say that stage responds to simplification. So simplify_onboarding is the direct fix for the measured problem, whereas promotional_pricing is a reaction to a competitor's move rather than to our own broken funnel. Verification triage: I verify memory_86 because it is the single belief my intended action rests on, and its recorded outcomes (completion rate, time-to-value, 'early adoption') are all upstream proxies — none of them is qualified revenue, which is the objective. If the archived record shows the lift never propagated past activation, the intended action is much weaker and I should reconsider. I verify memory_73 second because it is the strongest competing pull under competitive pressure and the least supported for this objective: 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' is silent on retention, margin, and whether the acquired price-sensitive SMB cohort persists — exactly the failure mode that converts short-term revenue into unsustainable revenue. I do not spend the budget on memory_31 (largely redundant with memory_86 on the same mechanism), memory_57 (referral is off-problem this week), memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist does not address an SMB/self-serve funnel decline), or memory_91 (supporting, not load-bearing). Downstream value risk: cutting signup fields and onboarding steps can lift activation while degrading lead qualification and downstream conversion quality, so the experiment must instrument qualified-pipeline and retention metrics, not just completion. I hold the inherited claims as probable-but-proxy-based rather than settled, which is why I run a measured standard experiment with downstream guardrails instead of a broad rollout, and why the verification results can still flip me toward promotional_pricing if memory_86 proves hollow and memory_73 proves durable.

final.rationale: Both verifications resolved cleanly and in the same direction. exp_86 came back stronger than the memory summary implied: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and crucially 30-day retention +3% — so the onboarding lift is not a pure upstream proxy, it propagated into retained accounts. That removes my main worry about memory_86 and makes simplify_onboarding well-supported for the sustainable-qualified-revenue objective, and it targets exactly the two metrics that are actually declining (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%). exp_73 came back the other way and vindicates spending the second pull on it: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% look excellent in the memory summary, but 30-day retention -12% and the archived conclusion state the acquired cohort does not survive first renewal. The summarized belief was materially misleading relative to a long-term objective, so promotional_pricing is now affirmatively ruled out as the response to the competitor rather than merely deprioritized — matching the competitor on price would buy a quarter of revenue and lose the cohort. The remaining directions stay off-problem: referral_incentive (memory_57) targets established customers rather than the broken self-serve funnel, and enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) does not address an SMB/self-serve decline. Residual uncertainty I am deliberately keeping: exp_86 tested shortening the onboarding flow, whereas memory_31's mechanism is cutting required signup fields — these are adjacent but not identical, and field-cutting is the variant that can degrade lead qualification. exp_86's retention evidence is also 30-day, which is shorter than the renewal horizon where exp_73's cohort failed. So I run a standard experiment on flow shortening, not broad rollout and not aggressive field removal, and I instrument qualified-pipeline quality and retention past 30 days alongside completion and activation rather than declaring the inherited result settled.
